newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban authorities, emigrants meet on Helms-Burton.
newsitem.headline: Cuban authorities, emigrants meet on Helms-Burton.

text.p: Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina on Saturday blasted U.S. legislation tightening the longstanding economic embargo on Cuba.
He called the 10-month-old legislation a "collection of stupidities" and said it was part of a "veritable crusade (by Washington) against the Cuban nation and people."
Robaina was speaking at the opening of a meeting in Havana of Cuban authorities and members of the Cuban exile community against the United States' Helms-Burton law.
Robaina said Helms-Burton aimed to place Cuban sovereignty under the "jurisdiction of the Congress and president of another country."

The two-day conference, which officials said was attended by about 150 exiles, reflected efforts by communist-ruled Cuba to drum up support against Helms-Burton and to draw closer to moderate sectors among the one million or so Cubans who live abroad, most of them in the United States.

Helms-Burton, approved by President Bill Clinton last March, was meant to increase pressure on President Fidel Castro by discouraging foreign investment in Cuba. It included provisions to punish foreign companies deemed to be benefitting from properties nationalised after Cuba's 1959 revolution.
It has been strongly criticised not just by Cuba but by U.S. allies such as Canada and the European Union.

Robaina urged moderate Cuban-Americans, whom he called the "silent majority," to make their voices heard and destroy the myth that "the policy of Washington towards Cuba is supported by all the Cuban community who live in the United States."
Cuba views Washington's policy toward it as being a product of links between right-wing sectors of U.S. Congress and hardline opponents of Castro in Miami.

In addition to sections on foreign investment, Cuba also objects strongly to other aspects of Helms-Burton that demand a radical reform of Cuba's one-party system as a condition for improved U.S.-Cuba relations. Ties between Washington and Havana have been hostile since Castro came to power.

Robaina said while it was clear Cuba had to prepare for further interference from Washington rather than an easing of tensions, Havana was still prepared to hold a dialogue with the United States. But this had to be "on the one condition that it is a dialogue without conditions, on a basis of equality and mutual respect," he said.

Cuba has held two conferences with the exile community since 1994 on the wider theme of drawing closer to them. Authorities have invited exiles to such meetings only on condition they held a "respectful" view of the island.

Previous conferences have been criticised by hardline exile opponents as gatherings of Cuban authorities and their friends abroad. Authorities have denied that, noting some participants at past conferences have been critical of Cuba's communist system.
